one_liner: Pure-Go image resizer with SSE2 assembly kernels for YCbCr, RGBA and Gray planes; faster than other pure-Go resizers.
what_it_does: Resizes Go image.YCbCr (subsampling 4:1:0 to 4:4:4), RGBA, NRGBA and Gray images into a caller-allocated destination of the same type, using bilinear, bicubic (B/C configurable, default B=0, C=0.5) or Lanczos filters. It can also convert YCbCr chroma subsampling (for example 4:2:2 to 4:2:0) and do field-aware resizes of interlaced video. The API is rez.Convert(dst, src, filter) for one-off calls, or PrepareConversion plus NewConverter for a reusable converter; it is a Go library, not a replacement for the ImageMagick command line or the golang.org/x/image/draw Scaler interface.
how_it_is_fast: It filters the decoded YCbCr planes directly instead of converting to RGBA first (imaging and gift convert), with a separable two-pass resize (vertical, then horizontal) driven by precomputed 14-bit fixed-point int16 kernels. Hot loops are generated SSE2 assembly per tap count (2 to 12, plus a generic N-tap path) built on PMADDWD multiply-accumulate with PUNPCKLBW/PACKUSWB widening and packing; the tests check that the assembly output is bit-identical to the pure-Go loops. Each plane is split into GOMAXPROCS horizontal slices run as goroutines, and a reusable Converter avoids rebuilding kernels and buffers for repeated geometry.
when_to_use: Go services that make thumbnails or scaled copies from JPEGs decoded with image/jpeg and must stay free of cgo; staying in YCbCr skips a full-resolution RGBA conversion.
Video or frame pipelines in Go that resize many frames of the same size (reuse one Converter per goroutine), including interlaced material and chroma-subsampling changes.
amd64 servers, where the SSE2 kernels are used; the filter widens on downscale (support divided by the scale factor), so even the bilinear setting is antialiased rather than point-sampled.
Vendoring a small, dependency-free MIT resizer into a Go codebase that cannot take new upstream maintenance.
when_not_to_use: Whenever cgo or an external process is acceptable: in the same i7 table ImageMagick -thumbnail with jpeg:size (0.057 s), the libvips binding (0.070 s), epeg (0.079 s), fastjpeg (0.082 s), OpenCV (0.110 s) and vipsthumbnail (0.115 s) all beat rez (0.349 s).
Large-reduction JPEG thumbnails: rez needs the full-resolution decode, while DCT-domain downscaling on load (jpeg:size, epeg, fastjpeg) skips most of the decode work.
arm64 and other non-amd64 targets: only SSE2 amd64 assembly exists (no AVX2, no NEON), so other architectures run the scalar Go loops.

Colour-accurate work: filtering runs on gamma-encoded 8-bit values (issue #8, open since 2015, unanswered), NRGBA is filtered as packed bytes without premultiplying alpha, and there is no 16-bit or float path.
Paletted, CMYK, RGBA64 or Gray16 images: anything other than YCbCr, RGBA, NRGBA or Gray returns 'unknown image format' (issue #12 hit this with a PNG).

integration.min_toolchain: CI was Go 1.5 to 1.8 (issue #9, 'Cannot build with Go >1.7', closed 2016); no go.mod, so modules use a pseudo-version. fawick/speedtest-resize's go.mod (go 1.26.0) still pins rez at the 2017-07-31 commit, which suggests it builds on current Go; not verified here
integration.platforms: amd64 with SSE2 assembly; any other Go target through the pure-Go fallback (scalers_gen.go)
integration.thread_safety: Convert starts its own goroutines (GOMAXPROCS slices by default, inline when Threads is 1). A Converter keeps its intermediate plane buffers between calls (converterContext.buffer), so one Converter must not be used from several goroutines at once; use one per goroutine.

gotchas: The destination must be pre-allocated at the target size with the same type and plane layout as the source; YCbCr-to-RGBA or other pack/plane mismatches return an error even though the docs say Convert applies 'any necessary colorspace conversion'.

One-shot rez.Convert rebuilds kernels and buffers on every call and defaults to GOMAXPROCS goroutines per call; under concurrent request load set ConverterConfig.Threads to 1 and reuse Converters to avoid oversubscription and repeated setup.

From kernels.go: horizontal kernel offsets are stored as int16 absolute pixel positions, so inputs wider than 32767 px would overflow (slice panic in Go, out-of-range reads in assembly); this was read from the source, not tested.
Planes smaller than 2 px in either dimension are rejected, and the assembly is disabled for outputs narrower than 16 px (pure-Go path used).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick rez only when the program must stay pure Go: if cgo or an external process is allowed, libvips, epeg and OpenCV were 3-6x faster in the same shootout, and fast_image_resize is the stronger SIMD choice in Rust (AVX2 and NEON).
verified_claims_summary: In fawick/speedtest-resize (third-party, MIT; run by contributor nono on a 3.4GHz Core i7 with Ubuntu 16.10, one pass over the first ten 5616x3744 JPEGs, decode plus resize plus encode timed together), rez_bilinear averaged 0.349 s per file against 0.568 s for ImageMagick `convert -resize 150x150>` and 0.370-0.515 s for the other pure-Go resizers, while ImageMagick's -thumbnail path took 0.057 s. Reading the harness adds three points to the verifier's notes: rez runs on all cores by default (GOMAXPROCS goroutines) and the harness sets no thread limits for any contender; its bilinear kernel widens to about 76 taps at this 37x reduction, so the resize itself is a real antialiased filter, and every pure-Go row also pays for a full Go image/jpeg decode; and the harness ignores decode and convert errors but still counts the file and its time, although rez's 0.140% average output size (other pure-Go rows: 0.146-0.160%) shows no sign that files were skipped.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit 2017-07-31 and archived 2024-05-19 (214 stars, one open issue). It is MIT-licensed with no dependencies, and small enough to vendor (a dozen Go files plus two generated assembly files), but it will get no fixes and has no SIMD outside amd64.
